title: Apply efficient time management to the work of a department/division/section

lessons.title: Planning and prioritising the section's work
lessons.html:
Why time management matters in the export season

In a packhouse or cold store during peak season, time is the scarcest resource. Fruit cannot wait, vessels sail on schedule, and inspections are booked for set times. A manager who manages time well protects fruit quality, controls overtime costs and reduces stress for the whole team.

Understanding where time goes

Start by analysing how time is spent. Keep a simple time log for yourself for a week, and observe how the section's time is used. Common time wasters include:

  • unplanned meetings and interruptions;
  • waiting: for forklifts, packaging, trucks or decisions;
  • rework caused by errors, such as remarking cartons;
  • unclear instructions leading to the wrong work being done;
  • searching for documents or information;
  • doing work that should be delegated.

Setting goals and priorities

  • Link daily work to the section's objectives, such as pack 40 000 cartons this week at Class 1 pass rate above target.
  • Use the urgent and important matrix: do urgent and important tasks now (a cold room alarm); schedule important but not urgent tasks (training, maintenance planning); delegate urgent but less important tasks; drop tasks that are neither.
  • Many crises in season come from important tasks that were never scheduled, such as preventive maintenance or packaging orders.

Planning tools

  • Season plan: expected volumes per week, staffing, packaging and cold storage needs.
  • Weekly schedule: packing programmes, inspections and container loadings.
  • Daily to-do list ranked by priority.
  • Shared calendar for meetings, audits and deadlines.
  • Gantt chart for projects such as preparing the packhouse before the season.

Build in buffers. Plan loadings with time for delays at the port or a late inspection, so one problem does not cascade into missed vessels.

lessons.title: Delegating, controlling interruptions and reviewing
lessons.html:
Delegation

A manager who tries to do everything becomes the bottleneck. Delegation frees time for planning and develops staff.

  1. Choose the task and the right person, considering skills and workload.
  2. Explain the task, the expected result, deadline and authority clearly.
  3. Provide resources and training.
  4. Agree on check-in points, without micro-managing.
  5. Review the outcome and give feedback and recognition.

You can delegate authority but you remain accountable for the result.

Controlling interruptions and meetings

  • Set times when you are available for questions, and protect time for planning.
  • Empower supervisors to make routine decisions within clear limits.
  • Hold short, focused meetings: a clear agenda, start and end on time, decisions and actions recorded with owners and dates. A ten-minute start-of-shift briefing often replaces many separate conversations.
  • Handle email in batches rather than constantly.
  • Keep documents and records organised, ideally in shared electronic folders, so information is found quickly.

Managing the section's time

  • Standard procedures reduce time spent explaining the same task.
  • Shift planning matches staff numbers to expected volumes.
  • Preventive maintenance scheduled outside peak times reduces breakdowns.
  • Coordination with receiving, cold store and dispatch prevents waiting.
  • Fatigue management: long hours increase errors and accidents; respect legal working hours and rest periods.

Reviewing and improving

At the end of each week, review the plan against what happened. Which tasks overran and why? What caused waiting time? Use the answers to improve next week's plan. After the season, hold a review with supervisors and record lessons for next year.

Example

A dispatch manager notices that loaders wait about an hour each morning for pallet lists. By agreeing that the cold store sends the list by 16:00 the previous day, the team starts loading on time, and evening overtime drops.

Key points

  • Analyse where time is wasted before trying to fix it.
  • Prioritise using the urgent and important matrix.
  • Plan with season, weekly and daily schedules, with buffers.
  • Delegate clearly and remain accountable.
  • Control interruptions, run short meetings and review results weekly.

quiz.question: In the urgent and important matrix, what should be done with important but not urgent tasks such as training?

options.text: Ignore them until they become urgent
